content: # Why Your Remote Images Fail in DomPDF and How to Fix It When integrating `dompdf` into a PHP project, generating PDFs is often straightforward until you try to embed external assets like logos or product images. A common stumbling block occurs when the generated PDF simply omits an image that exists in your HTML source. You might have already configured `DOMPDF_ENABLE_REMOTE` to `true` in your `dompdf_config.inc.php`, and your HTML markup looks perfectly valid: ```html ``` If the image still doesn't appear, the issue is rarely a missing configuration flag. Instead, it usually points to a fundamental misunderstanding of how `dompdf` handles file paths versus URL references, or where your files actually reside on the filesystem. ## The Misconception of Remote Loading The `DOMPDF_ENABLE_REMOTE` directive controls whether `dompdf` will attempt to fetch images via HTTP/HTTPS from external web addresses (e.g., `https://example.com/logo.png`). Setting this flag to `true` is necessary for remote URLs, but it does not automatically enable the loading of local files based on relative paths. In your specific example, `src="logoweb.png"` is a relative path. When you run your script from a web server context (like Apache or Nginx), this path is resolved relative to the document root or the current execution directory, depending on how the script is invoked. `dompdf` often struggles to resolve these paths correctly if it is not given an absolute filesystem path or if the working directory changes during the rendering process. Even with `DOMPDF_ENABLE_REMOTE` enabled, `dompdf` will not automatically scan your project's `public/` folder or `assets/` directory just because you specified a relative filename. It expects either an absolute URL for remote resources or a precise absolute path to local files if you are configuring the loader differently. ## Ensuring Absolute Paths and Correct Directory Structure To resolve this, you must ensure that `dompdf` can unambiguously locate `logoweb.png`. The most reliable approach is to serve images via a public URL rather than relying on relative filesystem paths within the HTML string passed to `dompdf`. If your image is located at `/public/images/logoweb.png`, your HTML should reference it as: ```html ``` This guarantees that `DOMPDF_ENABLE_REMOTE` will handle the retrieval correctly. Alternatively, if you prefer to keep the file local, you must pass an absolute path in your PHP code when rendering the HTML: ```php $dompdf->loadHtml(''); // Or configure the base path in dompdf_config.inc.php if using relative paths ``` Another frequent pitfall is the location of `logoweb.png` itself. If your script runs from a CLI environment (using `php artisan` or a command-line runner) rather than through the web server, the "current directory" might be different than expected. In such cases, `dompdf` cannot resolve relative paths like `logoweb.png` unless you explicitly define the base path in your configuration or use absolute paths in the HTML. ## Security Implications and Best Practices Enabling remote loading is a double-edged sword. While it allows dynamic image fetching, it opens your renderer to potential security risks if not managed carefully. If `DOMPDF_ENABLE_REMOTE` is true, an attacker could theoretically inject malicious scripts into an external image source (like a data URI) if the server allows it. It is best practice to whitelist specific domains or ensure that all images are served over HTTPS. Additionally, consider using base64-encoded images for small assets like logos to avoid network requests entirely and eliminate path resolution issues: ```html ``` This method embeds the image directly into the PDF, removing any dependency on external servers or filesystem paths. For developers building complex applications on Laravel, managing assets is a core part of the workflow. If you need to dynamically generate PDFs containing company branding, consider leveraging services like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) that provide robust asset management solutions or pre-configured PDF rendering environments designed to handle these edge cases out of the box. Ultimately, the fix lies in ensuring `dompdf` has a definitive location for your image, whether through an absolute URL, a base64 string, or a correctly resolved absolute path.
